questions.text: What is the primary legal mechanism requiring government to obtain community approval before implementing housing projects affecting Indigenous Peoples?

options.text: Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC) — a legal requirement under RA 8371
Community consultation as a courtesy before project approval, which is often encouraged but not legally binding
Majority vote by municipal council members, which may influence decisions but does not specifically address Indigenous Peoples' rights
Environmental impact assessment sign-off only, which focuses on environmental factors rather than community consent

rationale.a: RA 8371 (Indigenous Peoples Rights Act, 1997) mandates FPIC for any project affecting IP ancestral lands/resources. FPIC is a legal requirement, not a discretionary courtesy. It requires full IP community participation and meaningful consent.
rationale.b: Consultation is necessary but insufficient; FPIC is the legal standard.
rationale.c: Municipal council vote is separate from FPIC; both may be required but FPIC targets IP communities specifically.
rationale.d: EIA is procedurally important but does not substitute for FPIC.
rationale.correct: RA 8371 (Indigenous Peoples Rights Act, 1997) mandates FPIC for any project affecting IP ancestral lands/resources. FPIC is a legal requirement, not a discretionary courtesy. It requires full IP community participation and meaningful consent.
rationale.takeaway: RA 8371: FPIC required before any project affecting IP lands/resources. This is a legal requirement.

questions.text: An Indigenous Peoples community faces relocation due to a government development project. Under RA 8371, which housing provision is mandatory?

options.text: Priority relocation within ancestral territory if possible; if not, compensation and benefit-sharing agreements are mandatory
Relocation to the nearest available government site, regardless of location, ensuring minimal disruption to community life.
Immediate conversion to urban formal housing away from traditional lands, focusing on modern amenities.
Community may be relocated without housing provisions if adequate warning is given, which is not typically the case.

rationale.a: RA 8371 prioritizes in-territory relocation when possible (preserves ancestral connection). If external relocation is unavoidable, benefit-sharing and compensation agreements are mandatory. This reflects IP rights to land and culture.
rationale.b: Nearest site ≠ RA 8371 priority; ancestral territory is preferred.
rationale.c: Forced conversion to urban housing violates RA 8371 community rights.
rationale.d: RA 8371 mandates housing provisions for relocated IPs.
rationale.correct: RA 8371 prioritizes in-territory relocation when possible (preserves ancestral connection). If external relocation is unavoidable, benefit-sharing and compensation agreements are mandatory. This reflects IP rights to land and culture.
rationale.takeaway: RA 8371 relocation: ancestral territory preferred; if not, benefit-sharing required.

questions.text: Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) housing programs must include which mandatory accessibility features?

options.text: Aesthetic design features and modern decoration only, which do not address accessibility needs
Wheelchair ramps, grab bars, accessible toilets, and appropriate door widths (minimum 85 cm clear)
Ground-floor units only (no multi-story buildings allowed), which limits housing options
Segregated community design separate from non-PWD populations, which is not inclusive

rationale.a: Aesthetics do not address accessibility function.
rationale.b: RA 7277 (Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, 1992) mandates universal accessibility design: ramps (maximum 1:20 slope), grab bars in toilets, accessible toilet design (seat height, space), doors ≥ 80cm width. These are practical, testable standards.
rationale.c: Multi-story buildings are permitted if equipped with elevators/ramps to access all floors.
rationale.d: RA 7277 emphasizes community integration, not segregation.
rationale.correct: BP 344 (Accessibility Law of 1983) and 2024 IRR mandate accessibility features: ramps (max 1:20 slope), grab bars in toilets, accessible toilets, doors minimum 0.85m width (Sec 5.2.1.2). These are practical, testable standards.
rationale.takeaway: PWD housing: universal accessible design mandatory (ramps, grab bars, accessible toilets, door widths).

questions.text: Why is livelihood restoration emphasized as a critical component in post-disaster housing programs?

options.text: To comply with international humanitarian law requirements, ensuring that all aspects of recovery, including economic stability, are addressed
To prevent relocated families from experiencing economic collapse and returning to original hazard areas
To increase government revenue from relocated communities, which can be reinvested into further development projects
To reduce dependency on housing subsidies, encouraging self-sufficiency and long-term economic resilience

rationale.a: Humanitarian law is relevant but not the primary reason tested.
rationale.b: Post-disaster housing failure occurs when livelihood is not restored. Relocated families in distant sites without job access often face economic collapse and may return to dangerous original sites or migrate elsewhere. Livelihood restoration ensures resettlement is sustainable.
rationale.c: Housing programs are not revenue-generating; this is not the rationale.
rationale.d: Subsidy reduction is not the primary goal.
rationale.correct: Post-disaster housing failure occurs when livelihood is not restored. Relocated families in distant sites without job access often face economic collapse and may return to dangerous original sites or migrate elsewhere. Livelihood restoration ensures resettlement is sustainable.
rationale.takeaway: Post-disaster livelihood restoration = sustainability. Without it, resettlement fails.

questions.code_citation: RA 10121 (DRRM Act); World Bank Post-Disaster Recovery

questions.text: What distinguishes disaster-affected housing programs from standard relocation-based resettlement?

options.text: Disaster housing is temporary; standard relocation is permanent, which affects the long-term planning of communities
Disaster housing uses only NHA; standard relocation uses only private developers, which is not a typical practice
Disaster housing prioritizes speed of delivery and livelihood restoration; standard relocation emphasizes infrastructure completeness
Disaster housing is voluntary; standard relocation is mandatory, which impacts resident participation

rationale.a: Disaster housing can be permanent if well-planned; temporariness is not the defining feature.
rationale.b: Both use mixed financing (NHA, private, government, community).
rationale.c: Disaster housing = crisis response requiring immediate shelter provision (temporary or transitional) PLUS rapid livelihood restoration. Standard relocation is deliberate, infrastructure-focused. Post-Yolanda experience showed failure when livelihood restoration was neglected.
rationale.d: Both involve varying degrees of community choice/coercion.
rationale.correct: Disaster housing = crisis response requiring immediate shelter provision (temporary or transitional) PLUS rapid livelihood restoration. Standard relocation is deliberate, infrastructure-focused. Post-Yolanda experience showed failure when livelihood restoration was neglected.
rationale.takeaway: Disaster housing = speed + livelihood. Standard relocation = infrastructure-focused.

questions.text: The principle of universal accessible design (as mandated for PWD housing under RA 7277) differs from 'special PWD-only housing' in that universal design:

options.text: Is more expensive to implement than segregated facilities, often requiring additional budget allocations for compliance
Benefits PWDs while remaining equally usable by non-disabled residents and visitors (ramps, accessible entry, grab bars serve everyone)
Is limited to PWDs only; non-disabled residents cannot use universal design features, which are specifically tailored for accessibility
Eliminates the need for specialized health services in housing, assuming all residents have equal access to external healthcare facilities

rationale.a: Universal design can cost less than segregated facilities (integrated systems are efficient).
rationale.b: Universal design = accessibility that benefits PWDs AND all other residents (parents with strollers use ramps; elderly users benefit from grab bars; everyone benefits from accessible entries). It integrates rather than segregates.
rationale.c: Contrary to universal design principle; features serve all users.
rationale.d: Universal design is about environment/facilities; specialized health services are separate program elements.
rationale.correct: Universal design = accessibility that benefits PWDs AND all other residents (parents with strollers use ramps; elderly users benefit from grab bars; everyone benefits from accessible entries). It integrates rather than segregates.
rationale.takeaway: Universal accessible design: benefits PWDs + all residents. Integration over segregation.

questions.code_citation: RA 7277 (Magna Carta for Disabled Persons); Universal Design Principles

questions.text: Which combination of features best characterizes a comprehensive special housing program for disaster-affected populations?

options.text: Temporary shelter only; permanent housing deferred to future budget cycles without interim livelihood support
Permanent housing only; no temporary shelter or interim support during the transition and reconstruction period
Temporary shelter rapidly provided + transition to permanent housing + livelihood restoration + hazard-aware site selection
Housing provision + mandatory relocation to government-designated remote sites without community consultation or livelihood programs

rationale.a: Temporary-only approach leaves families in limbo; violates RA 10121 recovery mandates.
rationale.b: Permanent-only delays ignores emergency shelter crisis.
rationale.c: Comprehensive disaster housing = immediate emergency shelter PLUS structured transition to permanent units PLUS livelihood restoration planning PLUS hazard-aware siting (not replicate original hazard). Post-Yolanda experience validated this multi-component model.
rationale.d: Remote relocation without livelihood causes program failure.
rationale.correct: Comprehensive disaster housing = immediate emergency shelter PLUS structured transition to permanent units PLUS livelihood restoration planning PLUS hazard-aware siting (not replicate original hazard). Post-Yolanda experience validated this multi-component model.
rationale.takeaway: Disaster housing = immediate + permanent + livelihood + hazard-aware. All four necessary.

questions.text: A proposed housing project will affect the ancestral lands of an Indigenous Peoples community. Which step must occur BEFORE project implementation under RA 8371?

options.text: Environmental impact assessment completion, which is crucial but not the first step
DHSUD project licensing, which is necessary but follows other approvals
City council zoning approval, which is important but not the initial requirement
Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC) from the IP community

rationale.a: EIA is important but procedurally secondary to FPIC.
rationale.c: Zoning approval is separate; FPIC targets IP communities specifically.
rationale.d: RA 8371 mandates FPIC BEFORE any project affecting ancestral lands. FPIC must precede all other approvals (zoning, licensing, EIA). It is the foundational legal requirement.
rationale.correct: RA 8371 mandates FPIC BEFORE any project affecting ancestral lands. FPIC must precede all other approvals (zoning, licensing, EIA). It is the foundational legal requirement.
rationale.takeaway: RA 8371 sequence: FPIC first, then other approvals follow.

questions.text: Senior Citizens housing under RA 9257 prioritizes proximity to which services?

options.text: Entertainment and recreational facilities only, which are considered essential for social engagement and mental health benefits
Government administrative offices, as they provide necessary services and support for senior citizens
Shopping malls and commercial districts, which offer accessibility to various goods and services needed for daily living
Healthcare facilities, pharmacies, and rehabilitation services

rationale.a: Recreation is beneficial but not the priority identified by RA 9257.
rationale.b: Administrative proximity is not relevant to senior housing needs.
rationale.c: Commercial proximity is not a RA 9257 senior housing requirement.
rationale.d: RA 9257 (Senior Citizens Act, 2003) mandates housing proximity to healthcare, pharmacies, and medical/rehabilitation services. Senior populations depend on frequent healthcare access.
rationale.correct: RA 9257 (Senior Citizens Act, 2003) provides privileges for seniors including priority access to housing near services, but specific mandates are under DHSUD senior housing guidelines. Senior populations depend on frequent healthcare access.
rationale.takeaway: Senior housing: healthcare/pharmacy/rehab service proximity mandatory (RA 9257).

questions.text: Compared to general housing programs, special housing programs in the Philippines are characterized by:

options.text: Larger funding allocations and higher construction volumes, often supported by international aid
Exclusive use of private developer financing, with minimal government intervention
Smaller scale, more specialized design, tailored to specific population needs, but often underfunded relative to need
Absence of government involvement; purely community-managed, relying on local resources and volunteer efforts

rationale.a: Special programs receive SMALLER allocations than mainstream programs.
rationale.b: Special programs use mixed financing (government, community, private).
rationale.c: Special programs (IP, PWD, senior, disaster) are smaller-scale, highly specialized, and often chronically underfunded. They address legitimate needs but compete for resources with mainstream socialized housing.
rationale.d: Government has legal obligations (FPIC, accessibility standards); not purely community-managed.
rationale.correct: Special programs (IP, PWD, senior, disaster) are smaller-scale, highly specialized, and often chronically underfunded. They address legitimate needs but compete for resources with mainstream socialized housing.
rationale.takeaway: Special housing programs: specialized but underfunded relative to population need.

questions.code_citation: Philippine Housing Policy Review; DHSUD Budget Analysis
